Black-Body Radiation and Planck's Quantum
A glowing poker started a revolution

Heat an iron poker. First it glows dull red, then orange, then white-hot. Every hot object does this, and the colour depends only on temperature, not on what it is made of. In 1900 nobody could explain that glow with the best physics of the day. The fix needed one strange idea: energy comes in lumps . That idea is the seed of all quantum theory, and of lasers, chips and MRI scanners.
What is a black body?

Physicists wanted a clean test case: a "black body" that absorbs all light that falls on it and gives off only its own heat glow. A small hole in a closed oven is a good model. Light enters, bounces around and rarely escapes, so the hole looks black when cold. When the oven is hot, the hole glows with a universal colour pattern. Gustav Kirchhoff named the idea in 1860. By the 1890s careful measurements in Berlin gave the exact curve: brightness against wavelength. It rises, peaks, then falls. Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths (Wien's law). The Sun, near 5,800 K, peaks in the visible range.
The "ultraviolet catastrophe"

Classical physics treated the oven's light as waves. Short waves are easier to fit inside the box in huge numbers, and each wave mode was given an equal share of heat energy. Rayleigh and Jeans worked this out (1900-1905). The result: infinite energy at short wavelengths. A hot oven would pour out unlimited ultraviolet and X-rays. Paul Ehrenfest later called this the "ultraviolet catastrophe". Reality does the opposite: the glow fades at short wavelengths. Teal is what we measure. Red dashed is what old physics predicted.
Energy in lumps

Max Planck, in December 1900, found a formula that matched the data perfectly. To justify it he made an assumption he called an "act of desperation": the tiny oscillators in the oven wall can only swap energy in whole packets. The rule E = h × f. A packet of energy (a "quantum") equals frequency f times a tiny constant h, now called Planck's constant (about 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds). High-frequency (short-wave) packets are big. At a given temperature there is rarely enough energy to make one, so they are rare. That kills the ultraviolet catastrophe.
Paying only in coins

Imagine a shop where you can pay only in coins of fixed size, and the coin for blue light is worth much more than for red light. A customer with a small budget can easily pay many red coins, but hardly ever one expensive blue coin. So red glow is common, blue glow is scarce, and ultraviolet is rarer still. Where the analogy breaks: coins exist whether or not you spend them. Planck did not claim light itself was lumpy; he only claimed the exchange of energy was. Einstein took the bolder step in 1905 (next lesson).
Why we never notice

h is so small that a swinging playground child receives energy in packets far too fine to notice. The steps are there, but invisible, like the individual grains in a smooth-looking sand dune. This is a pattern in quantum physics: the strangeness is real but hides in the tiny. Ordinary life is the blurred average of enormous numbers of quanta.
The sky confirms Planck

Planck's law has been tested to extreme accuracy. The best black body ever measured is not in a lab but the whole universe. The NASA COBE satellite (FIRAS instrument, 1990) measured the leftover glow of the Big Bang, the cosmic microwave background. It matched a Planck curve at 2.725 K so precisely that the error bars were thinner than the line on the graph. John Mather shared the 2006 Nobel Prize for this. Astronomers also read star temperatures from their colour, using the same curve. Planck got the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Myths to drop

"Planck knew he had discovered quantum theory." No. He saw it as a trick for the maths and spent years trying to avoid it. "Quantum means very small." Not exactly. It means energy (and other things) come in steps. The whole Sun glows by this law. "The theory was proved wrong because old physics failed." Old physics still works for big, warm things. It fails when steps matter.
S.N. Bose and the photon gas

In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose, a lecturer at Dhaka University, derived Planck's law in a new way. He counted light quanta as identical and used pure counting, with no help from the old wave theory. Many referees would not take it. Bose sent the paper to Einstein, who translated it into German and had it published in the Zeitschrift fuer Physik. Bose's counting method became Bose-Einstein statistics , and particles that follow it are called bosons . It was the first time the quantum rule was derived from first principles.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Classical physics predicted infinite ultraviolet glow; reality does not. Planck (1900): energy swaps in packets E = hf. Bose (1924) gave a cleaner derivation; the CMB (COBE, 1990) is the best black body measured. Think about it Why does the packet idea reduce blue light more than red light? Why do we not see steps in the glow of a cooking stove?
The Photoelectric Effect and Einstein
Why your phone camera works

Shine light on some metals and electrons fly out. This is the photoelectric effect. It powers light sensors, solar cells and digital camera chips. It was also the effect that forced Einstein, in 1905, to say something shocking: light itself arrives in packets. That earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize, not relativity.
What was seen

Heinrich Hertz noticed in 1887 that ultraviolet light helps sparks jump. Philipp Lenard (1902) measured it carefully. Light knocks electrons out of a metal surface. Then came three odd facts. Below a certain colour (frequency), no electrons come out, however bright the light. Above it, electrons come out instantly , even with dim light. Brighter light gives more electrons, but not faster ones. Only a bluer colour gives faster electrons.
What the wave picture expected

If light is a smooth wave, a brighter wave carries more energy and should shake electrons out harder. Dim light should work eventually, just slowly, as the electron soaks up energy like a bucket under a drip. Colour should not matter much. The data said the opposite: colour decided everything, brightness only the count. The wave picture had no answer.
Light as packets

In 1905 Einstein took Planck's idea seriously: light itself is made of packets, each with energy hf. One packet hits one electron, all or nothing. The equation in words Kinetic energy of the electron = packet energy (hf) minus the "work function" W, the fee the metal charges to let an electron go. Red packets are too small to pay the fee, so no electron escapes, however many red packets arrive. Blue packets can pay, and any extra becomes speed. Brightness only means more packets, so more electrons.
Vending machine

A vending machine wants a 10-rupee coin. Pouring in a thousand 1-rupee coins will not work, but one 10-rupee coin works at once. Colour is the coin size; brightness is how many coins you have. Where it breaks: a machine can accept several small coins added up. An electron almost never accepts two small photons at once (only in very intense laser light).
Millikan tries to disprove it

Einstein's claim was so strange that Robert Millikan spent about ten years (1914-1916) building careful vacuum experiments to refute it. He measured the electron energy against light frequency and found a straight line exactly as Einstein predicted, and used its slope to get Planck's constant. He admitted the result, and won the 1923 Nobel Prize partly for this. Then in 1923 Arthur Compton showed X-rays bounce off electrons like billiard balls with definite momentum, so the packets (later named photons ) really behave like particles.
Wave and particle together

Light still shows waves: it makes interference patterns (Young, 1801). So light behaves as a wave when travelling and as lumps when exchanging energy with matter. Modern theory (quantum field theory) says it is neither a classical wave nor a classical ball but something new that shows each face in different experiments. The honest summary: the mathematics is clear and tested; the plain-language picture is always a compromise.
Myths to drop

"Einstein won the Nobel for relativity." The 1921 prize cited his law of the photoelectric effect. "Brighter light means more energetic photons." No. Brighter means more photons. Energy per photon depends on colour. "Photons are tiny marbles." They have no sharp position when travelling; the particle side shows up only on detection.
Raman and the photon

C.V. Raman discovered in 1928 that when light scatters from molecules, a little of it comes back with a changed colour. In photon terms, a photon gave some energy to the molecule (or took some) and left with less (or more). That is the Raman effect , announced on 28 February 1928 with K.S. Krishnan; Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first for an Indian in science. India celebrates 28 February as National Science Day. Raman spectroscopy is now a standard way to identify materials, and it works because light comes in photons.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Photoelectric facts: threshold colour, instant action, speed set by colour not brightness. Einstein 1905: light comes in quanta of energy hf. Millikan confirmed it in 1914-16; Compton added momentum in 1923. Raman effect (1928) is photons trading energy with molecules. Think about it A very bright red lamp ejects no electrons from a metal, but a faint blue lamp does. Explain with photons. Why does a solar panel need light above a certain frequency?
Bohr's Atom and Spectral Lines
Atoms have fingerprints

Pass sunlight through a prism and you see a rainbow crossed with dark lines. Heat a gas and it gives bright lines of particular colours only. Each element has its own set, like a barcode. Why only certain colours? That puzzle led Niels Bohr in 1913 to the first quantum model of the atom, and it is how we know what distant stars are made of.
Two problems at once

Problem 1: the atom. Ernest Rutherford (1911, from Geiger and Marsden's gold-foil scattering) showed an atom has a tiny heavy nucleus with electrons far outside. But an electron circling a nucleus should radiate light, lose energy, and spiral in within a tiny fraction of a second. Atoms should collapse. They do not. Problem 2: the lines. Johann Balmer (1885) and Johannes Rydberg (1888) found simple number patterns in hydrogen's lines, but nobody knew why.
Allowed orbits only

Bohr (Denmark, 1913) made bold rules: An electron can orbit only in certain "allowed" levels. While in a level it does not radiate, ignoring classical physics. It can jump between levels, giving off or absorbing one photon whose energy equals the difference. A big drop means a high-energy photon (blue or ultraviolet); a small drop means red. Only certain drops exist, so only certain colours appear.
Hydrogen solved

Bohr's model produced the Balmer-Rydberg numbers for hydrogen exactly, including the value of the Rydberg constant from fundamental constants. The energy of level n in hydrogen is about -13.6 eV divided by n²: ground state -13.6 eV, then -3.4, -1.5, and so on. Light from the drop to level 2 is the visible Balmer series; the drop to level 1 is ultraviolet. This was a spectacular result for a model built in a few months.
Where the model broke

Bohr's picture treats the electron as a little planet. It fails for helium and heavier atoms, cannot explain why some lines are brighter, and cannot predict how atoms bond. It also never says why orbits are allowed. The answer came in 1924-26 (de Broglie, then Schrödinger): the electron is a wave, and only waves that fit around the nucleus survive. Bohr's orbits became fuzzy clouds called orbitals. Think of Bohr's model as a useful map that is not the territory.
Experiments that confirmed levels

Franck-Hertz experiment (1914). James Franck and Gustav Hertz fired electrons through mercury vapour. The electrons lost energy only in fixed chunks (4.9 eV), and the vapour glowed in ultraviolet, direct evidence of energy levels. They received the 1925 Nobel Prize. Stars. Dark lines in sunlight match elements on Earth. Helium was first spotted in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, long before it was found on Earth (1895). Bohr won the 1922 Nobel Prize.
Myths to drop

"Electrons orbit like planets." No. That is Bohr's picture, now replaced by probability clouds. "The electron slides smoothly between levels." The jump is not a path you can follow; it is a change of state. "Bohr's model is simply wrong." It is wrong in detail but right about the key idea: energy levels.
Helium in Guntur, Raman and Saha

The Sun's yellow line that revealed helium was observed during the total solar eclipse of 18 August 1868 by the French astronomer Pierre Janssen from Guntur, India. Norman Lockyer in England concluded it was a new element. Meghnad Saha (1920) used atomic levels to explain star spectra: hotter stars strip atoms of electrons, so the lines change. The Saha equation is the basis of stellar classification. C.V. Raman's effect (1928) also reads the vibration levels of molecules.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Atoms give light of only certain colours because electrons have only certain energy levels. Bohr (1913): photon energy equals the gap between levels. Franck-Hertz (1914) proved levels; Bohr's orbits were later replaced by orbitals, but the levels stayed. Think about it Why does a neon sign glow a different colour from a hydrogen lamp? Why was the "falling electron" problem such a worry for Rutherford's atom?
De Broglie and Matter Waves
If light can be a particle, can a particle be a wave?

By 1923 light had been shown to act like both wave and particle. A young French aristocrat-turned-physicist, Louis de Broglie, asked: if so, why should matter be different? His answer, in his 1924 PhD thesis, was that every moving particle has a wave. This is why electron microscopes work, and why atoms have fixed energy levels.
The de Broglie wavelength

The rule wavelength = h / momentum. Momentum is mass times speed. h is Planck's tiny constant, so for anything heavy the wavelength is absurdly small. A cricket ball at 40 m/s has a wavelength of about 10⁻³⁴ m, a billion billion billion times smaller than an atomic nucleus. So the ball never shows wave effects. An electron is about 10³⁰ times lighter, so its wavelength can be comparable to the spacing of atoms in crystals (a fraction of a nanometre). That is where waves become visible.
Why only certain orbits

De Broglie noticed that Bohr's allowed orbits are exactly those where a whole number of electron waves fit around the circle. If the wave does not fit, it cancels itself after a lap, like a badly timed push on a swing. This is the first explanation of why atoms have steady levels: it is the same maths as a guitar string, which can only vibrate in whole numbers of half-waves.
Ripples on a ring

Flick a ring of water and only some ripple patterns survive. Others fade. Quantum levels are the survivors. Where it breaks: the electron wave is not a ripple in some material. It is a wave of probability (see the wavefunction lesson), and it lives in an abstract space, not a ring you could photograph.
Electrons diffract

In 1927 at Bell Labs, Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer bounced electrons off a nickel crystal. They found an intensity pattern peaking at certain angles, the same signature as X-ray diffraction, matching de Broglie's wavelength. Independently, G.P. Thomson in Aberdeen sent electrons through thin metal foil and saw rings. De Broglie got the 1929 Nobel; Davisson and Thomson shared the 1937 Nobel. Interference has since been seen with neutrons, atoms and even large molecules: in 1999 Anton Zeilinger's group (Vienna) saw it with C60 "buckyballs" of 60 carbon atoms.
Seeing with matter waves

Microscopes are limited by wavelength: you cannot see detail smaller than the wave you use. Visible light is about 500 nm; fast electrons can have wavelengths thousands of times shorter. The electron microscope (Ruska and Knoll, 1931) shows viruses and atoms. Neutron beams likewise map magnetic and crystal structure.
Myths to drop

"Everything is a wave, so I could diffract through a door." Your wavelength is about 10⁻³⁶ m. Not possible. "The electron is smeared into a cloud of matter." Detectors find it at one spot; the wave tells the odds of where. "De Broglie proved it was a real wave in space." Experiments show wave-like patterns; what the wave is is an interpretation question.
Bose and de Broglie, Raman and Krishnan

Einstein championed S.N. Bose's 1924 photon counting; he then used the same counting for atoms and, reading de Broglie's thesis (shown to him by Paul Langevin), backed matter waves too. Schrödinger said he was led to his wave equation by Einstein's remarks on de Broglie. In India, electron microscopes now operate in IISc Bengaluru, TIFR and IITs, and the Raman group's early work on X-ray and light scattering tied waves and quanta together in the same decade.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

De Broglie (1924): wavelength = h / momentum. Davisson-Germer and G.P. Thomson (1927) showed electrons diffract. Standing waves explain Bohr's levels; big objects have unnoticeably short wavelengths. Think about it If you doubled an electron's speed, would its wavelength grow or shrink? Why? Why can an electron microscope see smaller things than a light microscope?
The Double-Slit Experiment
Feynman called it the one mystery

Richard Feynman said the double-slit experiment contains "the only mystery" of quantum mechanics. If you understand one experiment, make it this one. It needs no equations, only a screen with two slits. It shows in one go why quantum objects cannot be thought of as ordinary balls or ordinary waves.
With waves: stripes

In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw bright and dark stripes on a screen. Where wave crests from both slits meet, they add (bright). Where a crest meets a trough, they cancel (dark). This is interference , the fingerprint of waves. It convinced physicists that light is a wave.
With bullets: two heaps

Fire bullets through two slits and you get two heaps behind the slits. Each bullet takes one path, and the heaps simply add. No stripes. So the test is simple: stripes mean wave, two heaps mean particles.
Electrons, one at a time

Now fire electrons, so rarely that only one is in the machine at a time. Each makes a single dot on the screen, like a particle. But after thousands of dots the stripes appear! One electron cannot have been interfering with a neighbour. Each one seems to have gone through both slits as a wave and landed as a single dot.
Watch which slit, and the stripes vanish

Place a detector at the slits to see which one each electron uses. You find each goes through exactly one slit. But now the stripes disappear and you get two heaps. Finding the path destroys the interference. This is not clumsiness of the detector alone; any way of learning the path, even in principle, kills the stripes. Information is what matters.
What is known and what is interpretation

Known (every interpretation agrees) The probability of landing at a spot comes from adding two amplitudes (the wavefunction contributions of each path). Stripes arise when the paths are not recorded. Interpretation What the electron "really did": went through both (Copenhagen-style wave talk), split into many worlds, or followed a guided path (Bohm). Same predictions, different stories. Analogy breaks: the electron is not a splitting blob. You never see half an electron.
Key experiments

Young, 1801: light stripes. Davisson-Germer, Thomson, 1927: electron diffraction. Claus Joensson, 1961: electrons through real slits. Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi (Bologna, 1974) and Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi (1989): single electrons building stripes dot by dot. Arndt, Zeilinger and colleagues, 1999: stripes with C60 molecules; 2019: molecules of over 25,000 atomic mass units (Fein et al., Vienna and Basel).
Myths to drop

"The electron is aware of being watched by a conscious mind." No. Any physical record, even by a mindless atom, destroys the stripes. "The electron splits in two." It always lands whole. "Quantum eraser sends messages to the past." Erasing path information restores stripes only when the data is sorted afterwards. No signal goes backwards.
Quantum optics in India

Urbasi Sinha's group at the Raman Research Institute, Bengaluru, runs single-photon interference experiments. In 2010, with colleagues at Waterloo, she reported a triple-slit test of the rule that probabilities come from adding two-path contributions only (published in Science), finding no sign of extra terms. Such tests also support India's National Quantum Mission aims in photonics. S.N. Bose's photon counting (1924) is part of the same story: photons that are indistinguishable behave in ways ordinary balls cannot.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Single electrons land as dots but make stripes in the long run. Learning the path destroys the stripes. The maths is agreed; the story of what happened in between is debated. Think about it Why does the stripe pattern build up from single dots prove the stripes are not caused by electrons bumping each other? What would you expect if a slit were blocked after the electron passed it?
The Wavefunction and Probability
Nature rolls dice, but the dice are loaded

Quantum theory describes a particle by a wavefunction , written ψ (the Greek letter psi). It does not tell you where the particle is. It tells you the odds of finding it in each place. This was the moment physics gave up a perfectly predictable universe. Many people, including Einstein, never fully accepted it.
What the wavefunction is

De Broglie's matter wave and Schrödinger's equation (next lesson) describe a wave spread over space. But what is waving? Schrödinger first hoped it was a smeared-out electron. It could not be: electrons always show up as whole points. In 1926 Max Born made the key proposal. The wave is a wave of probability amplitude . At each place it has a size, and the size squared is the chance of finding the particle there. Born rule Probability density = |ψ|². Read as "the size of psi, squared". Born received a share of the 1954 Nobel Prize for it.
Odds, not positions

The tall part of the curve means the particle will probably be found there, but a single measurement gives one spot. Repeat many times with identical set-ups and the dots fill out the curve. The probabilities come out exactly right, always.
Why you add amplitudes, not odds

This is the core of quantum weirdness. Amplitudes can be positive or negative (really, they have a "phase"). When two possible paths lead to the same place, you add their amplitudes first, then square. Two equal amplitudes pointing the same way give four times the odds of one path. Pointing opposite ways, they cancel to zero odds. That is exactly the double-slit stripe pattern: dark stripes are where the two path amplitudes cancel. If paths are recorded, you add odds instead, and the stripes vanish.
The weather forecast

A forecast of "70% rain" gives odds. But in a weather forecast the odds reflect ignorance; the actual weather was decided. In quantum theory, standard thinking says there is no hidden decision to be ignorant of, at least not one that works locally (see Bell's theorem). Analogy breaks: weather odds never cancel each other out. Quantum amplitudes do.
Testing the Born rule

Every quantum experiment is a test: electron diffraction, spectra, transistors. A sharp special test: in 2010 Urbasi Sinha and colleagues at Waterloo used triple slits to check that no "third-order" interference exists. If Born's rule were wrong, a certain combination of patterns would not be zero. They found it to be zero within about 1%. Later experiments tightened this. What the wavefunction is (a real thing or a bookkeeping device) remains debated. The 2012 PBR theorem (Pusey, Barrett, Rudolph) constrains certain views, but not all.
After the click

When a detector finds the particle at a spot, the wavefunction is updated: now the particle is there, and a second measurement right after finds it at the same place. Textbooks call this "collapse". Whether collapse is physical or just updated knowledge is the measurement problem (later lessons).
Myths to drop

"The wavefunction is the electron smeared out." The electron always arrives whole. "Probability means quantum theory is vague." The odds are predicted to ten or more decimal places in some cases. "Einstein was wrong to say God does not play dice, so hidden variables are disproved." Bell showed that local hidden variables fail; others remain possible.
Probability and Indian physics

Indian physicists contributed to the statistical side of quantum theory. S.N. Bose's 1924 counting rule decides the odds for identical particles. E.C.G. Sudarshan's 1963 representation (with Roy Glauber, who won the 2005 Nobel for his part) describes light quantum states using probability-like functions, a tool in quantum optics today.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

ψ gives amplitudes; |ψ|² gives odds (Born, 1926). Add amplitudes first, then square: this makes interference. The mathematics is accepted; the meaning of ψ is debated. Think about it Why can two ways of reaching a spot give less chance than one way? How does a single click differ from the pattern after a thousand clicks?
Schrödinger's Equation (No Heavy Maths)
The rulebook of the small

Newton's laws tell a cricket ball where to go. Erwin Schrödinger's equation (Zurich, early 1926) does the same job for the wavefunction of an electron or atom: it tells you how ψ changes in time. From it we can compute the colours of atoms, the shapes of molecules and the behaviour of every chip in your phone. Schrödinger shared the 1933 Nobel Prize with Paul Dirac.
What it says

Schrödinger's equation The rate at which ψ changes in time depends on the energy of the system (its "Hamiltonian"): iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Hψ. In words: energy decides how the wave evolves. Like Newton's laws, it is deterministic : given ψ now, it fixes ψ later exactly. The randomness comes only at measurement, when Born's rule gives the odds. Two different rules: smooth evolution between, random jump at a click.
Why energy comes in steps

Confine a particle (like an electron in an atom) and the equation allows only waves that fit, like a guitar string with fixed ends. Each allowed wave has a definite energy: those are the energy levels. This is the maths behind de Broglie's idea.
It never stops moving

The lowest wave in a box still has some bend in it, so it has energy. A confined particle can never be perfectly at rest. The tighter the box, the higher this minimum energy. That is why atoms do not collapse: squeezing an electron closer to the nucleus raises its energy more than the electric attraction pays back. This "zero-point energy" is why liquid helium stays liquid even near absolute zero at normal pressure.
The first big win

Schrödinger solved the hydrogen atom in 1926. His levels matched Bohr's (-13.6 eV divided by n²) but also gave the shapes of the electron clouds (orbitals) and explained why some spectral lines are brighter. Hydrogen has an exact solution; for heavier atoms and molecules, computers give approximate answers. Quantum chemistry and drug design now rely on such computations.
Heisenberg got there first, differently

Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and Pascual Jordan had built a different looking theory in 1925, "matrix mechanics", using tables of numbers and no pictures. Schrödinger's waves looked friendlier. In 1926 Schrödinger showed they are mathematically equivalent. Dirac and John von Neumann later put both into one framework. Honest note: the equation is tested to extraordinary precision, but what ψ represents is the interpretation question.
Tests of the equation

Hydrogen spectrum to many decimal places. Molecular spectra, chemistry and bonding. Semiconductors: band structure comes straight from the equation and tells us which materials are chips or insulators. Atomic clocks, which depend on the exact energy levels. No experiment has contradicted it in its domain (slow, non-relativistic particles). Dirac extended it for speed close to light in 1928.
Myths to drop

"Schrödinger's equation says everything is random." It is perfectly predictable; the dice appear when measuring. "You need heavy maths to grasp it." The idea (waves, fit, energy) is simple; solving it is hard. "It was derived." It cannot be strictly derived from older physics; it was a guess that worked.
Raman spectra and Indian quantum chemistry

The levels of molecular vibration and rotation come from Schrödinger's equation, and the Raman effect (1928) reads them directly. Raman spectroscopy is used today in Indian labs from IISc and IACS Kolkata (Raman's own institute) to forensic and pharma testing. Quantum chemistry methods, built on this equation, drive materials research under India's National Quantum Mission.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Schrödinger's equation tells how ψ evolves in time, smoothly and exactly. Confinement gives standing waves, so energy levels and zero-point energy. Randomness enters only with measurement. Think about it Why does squeezing an electron into a smaller space raise its energy? How can a deterministic equation sit with random measurement results?
Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
The most quoted idea in physics

Werner Heisenberg's 1927 uncertainty principle is often misused to mean "you cannot look without disturbing". The real idea is deeper: some pairs of properties cannot both be sharp at once, even in principle. It explains why atoms are stable, why stars shine and why LIGO needs special light.
Position and momentum

The rule Δx × Δp ≥ ħ/2. Δx is the spread in position, Δp the spread in momentum (mass times velocity), and ħ is Planck's constant divided by 2π. Their product has a floor. In words: the more tightly you pin down where a particle is, the more spread out its momentum must be, and the reverse. Earl Kennard proved this exact form in 1927.
It is a property of waves

A short, narrow wave pulse is built by adding many different wavelengths together. Since wavelength means momentum (de Broglie), a narrow position needs a wide mix of momenta. A pure single-wavelength wave is spread forever, so its position is unknown. This trade-off is true of all waves: a short musical note has a blurry pitch.
A musical note

A very short click has no clear pitch; a long steady note has a clear pitch. Short in time means blurry in frequency. Quantum particles do the same with position and momentum. Where it breaks: a click has a definite time and a spread of frequencies we can analyse. Quantum uncertainty is not just our blurry measuring: a particle in such a state has no sharp value to find.
What it explains

Stable atoms. Squeeze an electron near the nucleus and Δp (so energy) grows. A balance gives the atom's size. Zero-point energy. Nothing can be perfectly still. Energy-time version. A short-lived state has a fuzzy energy, so excited states have a natural linewidth. Quantum fluctuations that seeded cosmic structure (in inflation theory).
Tests

Single-slit diffraction: narrower slit, wider spread of landing spots. This is the principle shown daily in labs. Heisenberg's original gamma-ray microscope thought experiment suggested measuring disturbs, but the modern view is that the spread belongs to the state itself. In 2012 teams in Vienna (Erhart et al., neutrons) and Toronto (Rozema et al., photons) tested a more careful version about measurement disturbance and found Heisenberg's original bound can be beaten for disturbance, while the proven spread relation always holds.
Myths to drop

"It is the observer effect." That is a separate idea. Uncertainty exists even with no measuring. "It is about clumsy instruments." Perfect instruments cannot beat it. "It allows free energy or breaking physics." Borrowed energy exists only within strict, tiny limits and cannot be used to run a machine. "It works on cricket balls too." Yes, but ħ is so small the blur is unmeasurable.
LIGO-India and squeezed light

Gravitational wave detectors like LIGO fight quantum limits. They use "squeezed light", which trades uncertainty in one property for the other, to see tinier ripples. India has approved LIGO-India (Union Cabinet, April 2023, about ₹2,600 crore) at Aundha in Hingoli district, Maharashtra, expected to operate in the early 2030s. Indian scientists at IUCAA Pune, RRCAT Indore and IPR Gandhinagar are partners.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Δx × Δp ≥ ħ/2: narrow position means wide momentum. It comes from wave nature, not from clumsy measuring. It keeps atoms stable and limits sensors such as LIGO. Think about it Why does a very short musical click have an unclear pitch? How does uncertainty stop an electron falling into the nucleus?
Superposition and Measurement
Both, until you look

A quantum object can be in a superposition : a blend of two or more possibilities at once. Not "one of them, we do not know which", but a real combination that gives different results from either alone. Then a measurement gives one answer, and we are left with a puzzle that has no agreed solution.
What it is

If a system can be in state A or state B, it can also be in a combination of both, with an amplitude for each (see the wavefunction lesson). A photon at a half-mirror is in "both paths" until recorded. An electron around an atom can be in two energy levels at once. What is not true: it is not "spinning fast between A and B", and not "we just do not know which".
Why it is more than ignorance

Send a photon through a half-mirror, let both paths recombine at a second mirror, and it always exits the same port, thanks to interference. That cannot happen if the photon took one hidden path (50-50 would result). The paths must interfere, so both are in play. This is the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, a tabletop double slit.
The click

When we measure, we always see one definite result, with odds from Born's rule. The superposition seems to turn into a single outcome, called "collapse". Between measurements Schrödinger's smooth equation applies; at measurements, something else happens. Why the two rules differ is the measurement problem . Known vs not Known: the odds, to great accuracy. Not agreed: whether collapse is real, or an appearance (many-worlds), or tied to knowledge.
The bomb tester

Elitzur and Vaidman (1993) proposed testing whether a bomb works without setting it off. A live bomb at one path of the interferometer destroys the stripes, which can reveal its presence, in some trials, without the photon ever touching it. Experiments (Kwiat et al., 1995) confirmed it. It shows that paths not taken have physical effects.
How big can it go?

Superpositions have been seen in larger and larger things: C60 molecules (1999), molecules above 25,000 atomic mass units (2019), and superconducting rings carrying current in two directions at once (Delft and Stony Brook, 2000). Superconducting circuits are the basis of today's quantum computers. No limit has been found, only a practical difficulty: the environment disturbs big things (see decoherence).
A watched pot

Frequent measurement can freeze a system. If you keep checking, each look resets the clock. The Quantum Zeno effect, named by Misra and Sudarshan in 1977, has been seen in cold atoms (Itano and colleagues, 1990). It is used in some quantum devices.
Myths to drop

"The cat is both alive and dead because it is unsure." That misreads it; see the cat lesson. "Measurement needs a human." Any interaction that records the information acts as a measurement. "Superposition means a particle is in two places, so I could be too." For large warm things the blending is wiped out in a flash.
Sudarshan and TIFR

E.C.G. Sudarshan (with B. Misra) named the quantum Zeno effect in 1977. At the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, R. Vijay's group builds superconducting circuits where qubits are held in superposition, one of the leading hardware efforts that feeds India's National Quantum Mission.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Superposition is a genuine blend, shown by interference. Measurement gives one result with Born-rule odds. What collapse really is stays unsettled. Think about it Why does stripes-at-the-output prove a photon took both paths? If you look every instant, why might the system stay frozen?
Spin and the Stern-Gerlach Experiment
A property with no everyday twin

Electrons have a built-in property called spin . It makes them tiny magnets, and it decides how atoms stack into the periodic table, how magnets work and how MRI scanners see inside the body. The experiment that revealed its strangeness, in 1922, was done before anyone knew what spin was.
Stern and Gerlach (1922)

Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach in Frankfurt sent a beam of silver atoms through a magnetic field that is stronger on one side. A little compass-like atom is pushed up or down according to which way its magnet points. If the atoms' tiny magnets pointed in random directions, you would expect a smear. Instead there were two clean spots. The magnetic direction is quantised: only two options.
Two answers only

Spin was named in 1925 by George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit, building on Wolfgang Pauli's "two-valuedness" of electrons (1924). Paul Dirac in 1928 showed it falls out of relativity. The electron has spin one-half: measured along any chosen direction, you find "up" or "down", never in-between. Analogy breaks: it is not a ball spinning. An electron as a tiny ball would need to spin faster than light to produce this magnetism. Spin is an intrinsic quantum property.
Sequential tests

Chain several Stern-Gerlach magnets. Pass only "up along z" atoms, then test sideways (x): 50-50 up or down. Now take the "x up" atoms and test z again: you again get 50-50 up/down, even though we had selected only "z up" before! The sideways test erased the earlier information. Spin along z and along x cannot both be sharp, like position and momentum (see the uncertainty lesson). This is a clean example of superposition: "up along x" is an equal mix of "z up" and "z down".
Bosons and fermions

Every particle has a fixed spin. Spin-half particles (electrons, protons, neutrons, quarks) are fermions . Particles with whole-number spin (photon: 1; Higgs: 0) are bosons . This difference rules whether particles can share a state (next lessons). A spin-half particle must be turned by two full circles (720°) to return to its starting state: an odd fact confirmed with neutrons in the 1970s.
Spin at work

MRI. Hydrogen nuclei (protons) have spin. In a strong magnetic field they line up; radio pulses flip them and the signals map tissue (Lauterbur and Mansfield, Nobel 2003). Hard drives and memory read magnetic spin (spintronics; Fert and Gruenberg, Nobel 2007). Qubits. Spin up/down can be a quantum bit.
Evidence

Stern-Gerlach with many atoms; fine splitting of spectral lines (Zeeman and fine-structure effects); electron-spin resonance; the structure of the periodic table. Stern received the 1943 Nobel for this work, and Rabi the 1944 Nobel for magnetic resonance of spins.
Myths to drop

"Spin means rotating." It behaves like angular momentum, but nothing spins. "The up/down direction is built in before measuring." The sequential test shows it is not. "Particles with spin-zero have no properties." They simply lack that magnetism.
Bose and bosons

Particles with whole-number spin are named bosons after S.N. Bose, the name coined by Paul Dirac. Bose's counting for photons (spin 1) applies to all of them. Nuclear magnetic resonance and MRI are widely used in India, and spin-based quantum devices are a research thrust in NQM hubs at IIT Bombay (sensing) and TIFR.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Stern-Gerlach (1922): silver atoms split into two spots, so magnetic direction is quantised. Spin is intrinsic, not a spinning ball. Spin along different axes cannot both be sharp. Think about it Why does a second test along z give 50-50 again after an x test? Why can an electron's spin not be due to a literally spinning ball?
Quantum Tunnelling
Walking through a wall

Roll a ball at a hill without enough speed and it rolls back. A quantum particle, with a small chance, turns up on the far side. This tunnelling is why the Sun shines, how a smartphone stores your photos, and how we see single atoms.
A wave does not stop dead

A particle is described by a wavefunction. Meeting a barrier it cannot climb over (not enough energy), the wave does not drop to zero inside; it fades out gradually, like sound leaking through a thin wall. If the barrier is thin enough, some wave is still there on the other side. By Born's rule that means a real chance to find the particle there.
What controls it

The chance falls steeply (exponentially) with the barrier's thickness and height, and with the particle's mass. Light particles like electrons tunnel easily; protons much less; a cricket ball essentially never (its chance is many, many times smaller than one in any number you could write down). No energy is stolen. The particle does not climb the barrier; it appears beyond it with its original energy, but a smaller amplitude.
First great use: alpha decay

In 1928 George Gamow (and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon) explained alpha decay. An alpha particle is trapped inside a nucleus by a barrier, yet occasionally escapes by tunnelling. Wildly different half-lives (from microseconds to billions of years) follow from small differences in barrier thickness. This was an early, striking triumph of quantum theory.
Why stars burn

Two protons must get very close to fuse, but they repel. At the Sun's core (about 15 million K) classical physics says they would almost never touch. Tunnelling lets them fuse far more often. Without it the Sun would not shine at its current temperature and life would not exist. Gamow and others applied it to stars in the 1920s-30s.
Machines that tunnel

Scanning tunnelling microscope. Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer (IBM Zurich, 1981; Nobel 1986) measure the faint current that tunnels between a sharp tip and a surface. It maps single atoms. Flash memory traps electrons by tunnelling through thin insulators. Tunnel diode (Leo Esaki, 1957; Nobel 1973). Superconducting qubits use the Josephson junction, a tunnelling barrier.
Nobel 2025

In 2025 the Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for showing quantum tunnelling in an electrical circuit large enough to hold in the hand (experiments in the mid-1980s). It proved tunnelling is not just for atoms but works for a whole circuit, and paved the way for superconducting quantum computers.
Myths to drop

"The particle digs through." There is no path inside the barrier. The wave simply has some size beyond it. "Tunnelling is faster than light." Debated measurements of tunnelling time have not allowed signals faster than light. "I could tunnel through a wall." The odds are absurdly tiny.
Tunnelling in Indian labs

Scanning tunnelling microscopes are used in research at TIFR, IISc and the IITs to study new materials, including graphene and superconductors. Tunnelling junctions are the heart of the superconducting circuits being built in India under the National Quantum Mission.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Waves leak into barriers, so particles may appear beyond them. It explains alpha decay (Gamow, 1928) and fusion in the Sun. It powers STM, flash memory and superconducting qubits; 2025 Nobel Prize recognised it in circuits. Think about it Why do electrons tunnel more easily than protons? What would happen to the Sun's output without tunnelling?
The Quantum Atom: Orbitals and the Pauli Principle
Why the periodic table has its shape

Chemistry is the study of how atoms hold together, and it is all about electrons. Why do sodium and potassium behave alike, and neon and argon never react? Quantum theory answers: electrons live in orbitals, and a rule from Wolfgang Pauli (1925) forbids two of them from sharing the same state.
From orbits to clouds

Schrödinger's equation gives the electron in hydrogen a set of allowed standing waves. Each is an orbital : a cloud-shaped region showing where the electron is likely to be found (the size squared of its wavefunction). The ground state, "1s", is a sphere. Next come a sphere (2s) and three dumbbell shapes (2p), then five clover shapes (3d), and so on. The cloud is an odds map, not a path. Many electron "orbits" are replaced by "regions of likely find".
Quantum numbers

An electron state needs four labels: n (shell, sets size and energy), l (shape: s, p, d, f), m (orientation) and spin (up or down). Their allowed values follow from fitting waves, as in the guitar string picture. In an atom, each shell n has n² orbitals, so 2n² places for electrons: 2, 8, 18, 32.
No two in the same state

Electrons are fermions: no two can share all four labels. So each orbital holds at most two electrons, one spin up and one spin down. Pauli proposed this in 1925 to explain the structure of the table and anomalous spectra; he won the 1945 Nobel Prize.
Reading the table

Fill orbitals from lowest energy upward and you get the periodic table: row lengths 2, 8, 8, 18... Elements in one column share the number of electrons in their outer shell, so behave alike: lithium, sodium and potassium each have a single outer electron to give away. Noble gases have full outer shells and do not react. Bonds form when atoms share or swap electrons to fill shells.
A hotel with strict rooms

Imagine a hotel in which rooms come in set sizes and each room holds at most two guests of opposite habit. New guests take the cheapest free room. The outermost floor is what guests see, and it decides how they mix with other hotels. Where it breaks: electrons are identical and have no names. You cannot say which electron is in which room.
Why matter does not collapse

Pauli exclusion keeps atoms from squashing together and gives matter its volume. In 1967 Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that without it, ordinary matter would collapse to a tiny fraction of its size, and its size would not even scale with the amount of stuff. Your solidity is quantum.
Evidence

Atomic spectra show lines matching the predicted levels, with extra splitting from spin. Ionisation energies jump after a shell is emptied: a clear fingerprint of shells. In 2000s experiments, electron clouds of single atoms have been imaged directly, for example hydrogen orbitals using photoionisation microscopy (Stodolna et al., 2013).
Myths to drop

"Electrons orbit like planets." They form probability clouds. "Pauli is a force." It is a rule from the symmetry of identical fermions, not a push. "Orbitals are fixed solid shapes." They are odds maps that change when atoms bond.
Saha and Indian chemists

Meghnad Saha's 1920 ionisation equation used atomic energy levels to read stellar spectra. C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan's spectroscopy (1928) probes molecular energy levels. Indian quantum chemists such as Charusita Chakravarty and others work on computing orbitals for materials; the National Quantum Mission funds quantum materials work at IIT Delhi.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Orbitals are odds clouds with four labels (n, l, m, spin). Pauli (1925): no two electrons share the same state; each orbital holds two. Shell filling explains the periodic table and keeps matter from collapsing. Think about it Why are sodium and potassium chemically alike? What would the periodic table look like without the Pauli principle?
Bosons, Fermions and Bose-Einstein Condensates
Two kinds of particle

All identical particles in nature fall into two families that behave in opposite ways: fermions refuse to share a state, bosons love to. That single difference explains why matter is solid, why lasers exist, why stars do not collapse and why liquid helium creeps up walls.
No name tags

Two electrons are exactly identical, not just similar. Swap them and nothing changes. Quantum theory says the wavefunction of two identical particles either keeps its sign (bosons) or flips it (fermions) when they are swapped. If it flips, putting both in the same state would give zero: so fermions are barred from sharing. That is the Pauli principle.
Spin decides

Spin-half particles (electrons, protons, neutrons, quarks) are fermions. Whole-number-spin particles (photons, gluons, W and Z bosons, the Higgs) are bosons. Composite particles count: helium-4 (two protons, two neutrons, two electrons: six fermions) is a boson, helium-3 (five fermions) is a fermion. Paul Dirac named the two families after Bose and Enrico Fermi.
Bose, Einstein, Fermi, Dirac

In 1924 S.N. Bose derived Planck's law by counting identical light quanta. Einstein extended it to atoms (1924-25) and saw a strange consequence: cool enough, a gas of bosons would all fall into the lowest state. In 1926 Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac separately gave the rules for particles that obey exclusion.
A matter wave of its own

At extremely low temperatures, boson atoms pile into one quantum state and act as one giant matter wave. It was first made in 1995 by Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman (JILA, rubidium atoms, about 170 billionths of a kelvin above absolute zero) and by Wolfgang Ketterle (MIT, sodium). All three shared the 2001 Nobel Prize. This was 70 years after the prediction.
Same rule, many places

Superfluid helium-4 flows without friction below 2.17 K (Kapitza; Allen and Misener, 1937-38). Superconductors: electrons pair up into boson-like pairs (Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, 1957). Lasers: photons crowd into one mode. White dwarfs and neutron stars: fermion crowding resists gravity.
Fermions hold up the stars

When a star burns out, electrons squeezed together must occupy higher and higher states, which creates "degeneracy pressure", not from heat. This holds up white dwarfs. In 1930 the young Indian physicist S. Chandrasekhar, on a ship to England, calculated that above about 1.4 solar masses this pressure fails and a white dwarf must collapse. The Chandrasekhar limit explains supernovae of Type Ia. He shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Myths to drop

"Bosons are force particles and fermions are matter." A useful first rule, but composite bosons (helium-4) are matter too. "A condensate is a solid." It is an ultracold gas, not frozen. "Fermions repel each other by a force." It is a counting rule, not a push.
Bose, Chandrasekhar, and cold atoms

S.N. Bose gave his name to bosons and to Bose-Einstein statistics; he was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1954. S. Chandrasekhar (born in Lahore, 1910) made the fermion argument for stars. India's labs also work with ultracold atoms, for example at the Raman Research Institute, Bengaluru, and these skills feed quantum sensing and computing under the National Quantum Mission.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Fermions (half-integer spin) cannot share a state; bosons can. BEC: bosons pile into one state; made in 1995, Nobel 2001. Fermion crowding supports white dwarfs up to 1.4 solar masses (Chandrasekhar). Think about it Why is helium-4 a boson but helium-3 a fermion? How does the Pauli principle stop a white dwarf from collapsing?
Entanglement and the EPR Paradox
"Spooky action at a distance"

Two particles can be prepared so that their properties are linked, however far apart they go. Measure one and you instantly know the other. This entanglement puzzled Einstein for life, and is now the engine of quantum computing and secure communication.
What it is

Take two electrons made together with opposite spins. Their combined state is definite (total spin zero), but neither has its own spin before measuring. Measure one along any axis and you get "up" or "down" at random, and the other always gives the opposite along that same axis. Erwin Schrödinger named it "entanglement" (Verschraenkung) in 1935, calling it the characteristic feature of quantum theory.
The 1935 challenge

Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen published "Can quantum-mechanical description of physical reality be considered complete?" in 1935. Their argument, in plain steps: Distant measurements cannot disturb each other (locality). If you can predict a result with certainty without disturbing the system, then it has an "element of reality" (realism). By measuring Alice's particle you can predict Bob's without touching it. So Bob's particle had a definite value all along, and quantum theory, which lacks it, is incomplete.
The two gloves

Put a left and a right glove in two sealed boxes and mail them far apart. Opening one and seeing "left" tells you the other is "right". Nothing spooky: the glove was always left. EPR's hope was that entangled particles were like gloves: hidden values fixed from the start. Where the analogy breaks: Bell's theorem (next lesson) shows real particles cannot be that simple, once you test different measurement directions.
Bohr and the debate

Niels Bohr replied in 1935 that the very idea of "elements of reality" independent of the measurement set-up was too naive. For decades this seemed a matter of taste. Einstein, writing to Max Born in 1947, called it "spooky action at a distance" (spukhafte Fernwirkung). In 1951 David Bohm gave a simpler spin version, which is the one used in experiments.
Why relativity survives

Alice cannot use entanglement to send a message. Her own results are random; only when she later compares notes with Bob (by ordinary means, no faster than light) does she see the match. So no faster-than-light signalling occurs, and relativity is safe. Whether there is "something" travelling is the point of debate.
Experiments

Entangled photon pairs are made routinely (for example by shining a laser on a special crystal). John Clauser and Stuart Freedman (1972) and Alain Aspect (1982) tested them, and in 2015 several labs closed the gaps (see the Bell lesson). Entanglement has been spread over 1,200 km by China's Micius satellite (Yin et al., Science, 2017).
Myths to drop

"Entanglement sends information faster than light." It cannot. "Entangled particles are connected by a tiny wire." No signal-carrying link is found; the link is in the shared state. "Only exotic particles can be entangled." Photons, electrons, atoms, even diamonds and tiny drums have been.
Indian entanglement research

Indian groups at the Raman Research Institute (Bengaluru), the Harish-Chandra Research Institute (Prayagraj), the Indian Statistical Institute (Kolkata), IMSc Chennai and PRL Ahmedabad study entanglement in theory and experiment. The National Quantum Mission includes entanglement-based quantum communication, including satellite links, as a target.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Entangled particles share a state that is definite as a pair but not for each one. EPR (1935) argued quantum theory is incomplete; Schrödinger coined "entanglement". No usable signal is sent faster than light. Think about it How do the glove-in-a-box and entangled spins differ in what a test of other directions would show? Why can Alice not use her measurement to send Bob a message?
Bell's Theorem and the 2022 Nobel Prize
A debate settled by experiment

For 30 years after EPR, whether particles carry hidden "answers" from the start was thought to be a matter of philosophy. In 1964 John Bell, an Irish physicist at CERN, showed it can be tested . The tests say: no local hidden answers. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured the experimenters who proved it.
A game with two players

A source sends one particle of an entangled pair to Alice and one to Bob. Each randomly picks one of two settings (angles) for their detector and records a result: +1 or -1. They then compare many rounds and compute a combined score. The question: can any plan agreed in advance (like the gloves), with answers fixed at the source, beat a certain score?
The limit

Bell proved that if each particle carries pre-set answers and nothing travels between Alice and Bob (local realism), then correlations obey an inequality. The 1969 version by Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt (CHSH) is neat: the score S can be at most 2 for any local hidden plan. Quantum theory predicts up to 2√2, about 2.83 (the Tsirelson bound), for entangled particles measured at well chosen angles.
The two students

Two students in separate rooms get different questions and must give answers that match in some cases and mismatch in others. If they agreed a strategy beforehand, they can win at most 75% of rounds. With entangled particles they can win about 85%. It is not that they communicate; they cannot. It is that no pre-agreed strategy reaches that score. Where it breaks: students could cheat by signalling. In a real test, the choices are made too fast for any light-speed signal.
Experiments

Freedman and Clauser (1972) : first test, violated the inequality. Alain Aspect (1982) : switched detector settings while photons were in flight. Anton Zeilinger's group (Vienna) : many refined tests, and entanglement over long distances. 2015 loophole-free tests : Hensen et al. (Delft, electron spins 1.3 km apart), Giustina et al. (Vienna) and Shalm et al. (NIST). 2018 Big Bell Test : about 100,000 volunteers around the world chose the settings.
The 2022 prize

The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger "for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science". John Bell died in 1990 and never received one.
Known versus interpretation

Known No theory in which particles have pre-set answers and nothing influences distant results can match the data. Quantum theory fits. Interpretation Give up locality (Bohm's pilot wave), give up that a single outcome occurs (many-worlds), or give up "free choice" (superdeterminism, a minority view). Each is a different story. Nobody has to accept faster-than-light signals: Bell correlations carry no message.
Myths to drop

"Bell proved Einstein wrong about everything." Einstein was right that something must be added or given up. Bell showed which options remain. "It proves faster-than-light influence." Only if you assume realism. Other options exist. "The universe is not real." Only that local, pre-set values are ruled out.
Indian work on non-locality

Indian groups at ISI Kolkata, HRI Prayagraj, IMSc and RRI have worked on Bell inequalities and "device-independent" security, where certainty comes from a Bell violation alone. This underpins the quantum key distribution being developed under India's National Quantum Mission.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Bell (1964), CHSH (1969): local hidden values give S ≤ 2; quantum gives up to 2.83. Experiments (1972, 1982, 2015, 2018) violate the limit. 2022 Nobel: Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger. Think about it Why did Aspect change the detector settings during flight? Why does a Bell violation not let us send messages faster than light?
Interpretations: Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, Pilot Wave and More
One maths, many stories

Everyone agrees how to calculate with quantum theory. Almost nobody agrees what it says about reality. The disagreements are called interpretations . Be careful: most make the same predictions, so experiments cannot yet choose between them. Treat each as a story told about the same equations.
What needs explaining

Quantum theory has two rules: smooth evolution of ψ (Schrödinger) and a random jump at measurement (Born). What counts as a "measurement"? Why do we see only one result? Where does the quantum world end and the everyday world begin? Each interpretation answers differently.
Bohr, Heisenberg, and "shut up and calculate"

Developed around Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg, and aired at the 1927 Solvay conference. Core idea: ψ is a tool for predicting results; measurement results are what is real; do not ask what happens in between. Several versions exist, so "the Copenhagen interpretation" is loose. It treats collapse as basic and leaves the measuring apparatus unexplained. "Shut up and calculate" is a joking summary of the practical attitude.
Everett (1957)

Hugh Everett III proposed there is no collapse. ψ always evolves smoothly; when a measurement happens, the observer becomes entangled and all outcomes occur, each in its own branch. We only experience one branch at a time. Strength: simplest equations. Cost: a vast number of unseen branches, and a puzzle over what "odds" mean when everything happens.
De Broglie and Bohm

Louis de Broglie suggested it in 1927; David Bohm revived it in 1952. A particle has a definite position at all times and is steered by the wavefunction. It reproduces all standard predictions, and the "randomness" comes from not knowing the starting position. Cost: it is explicitly non-local (distant parts instantly guide each other), which Bell's theorem allows but which clashes with relativity's spirit.
More options

Collapse models (GRW, 1986; Penrose): collapse is a real physical process, rare for single particles and quick for big objects. These predict small differences and are testable ; so far experiments have ruled out some versions. QBism (Fuchs): ψ is an agent's personal degree of belief. Relational QM (Rovelli, 1996): properties exist only relative to other systems. Consistent histories and superdeterminism .
What is known

Bell tests rule out local hidden-variable theories, so every interpretation must be non-local, deny single outcomes, or deny free choice. Beyond that, the mainstream ones agree. In informal polls, no view has a majority. In a 2013 poll of about 30 specialists, Copenhagen led with about 40% (Schlosshauer, Kofler and Zeilinger). Collapse models are the first group to predict something different, and labs are testing them.
Myths to drop

"Many-worlds lets you travel between universes." Branches never communicate. "Consciousness causes collapse is mainstream." It is a rare minority view (von Neumann and Wigner raised it). "Experiments have proved Copenhagen." They have not chosen any.
Sudarshan and open questions

E.C.G. Sudarshan, one of India's most famous theorists, helped build the language used to describe measurement and decoherence in open quantum systems (GKSL equation, 1976, with Gorini, Kossakowski and Lindblad). The ancient "many ways of seeing" tradition in Indian philosophy is sometimes compared with interpretations, but those are analogies, not physics.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

All interpretations agree on predictions but tell different stories. Copenhagen (collapse), many-worlds (branches), pilot wave (particles plus guide), collapse models (testable). Bell tests narrow the choices but do not pick one. Think about it Which interpretations keep a single definite world, and what do they give up? Why are collapse models more scientific in the sense of testing than others?
Schrödinger's Cat and Decoherence
The most famous animal in physics

Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat in 1935 to show how absurd it seems if quantum rules are stretched to everyday things. Today the question it raises, why we do not see everyday superpositions, has a partial answer called decoherence , and it is the biggest obstacle for building quantum computers.
The cat in the box

A cat sits in a sealed box with a vial of poison that is released if one radioactive atom decays. The atom is in a superposition of "decayed" and "not decayed" until observed. If quantum rules apply all the way up, the cat is a superposition of alive and dead. Schrödinger did not think this was true. He meant it as a challenge: the theory, taken literally, seems silly at large scales. It was a thought experiment; no one has put a cat in a box this way.
Where does quantum end?

The theory has no built-in size limit. Yet we never see a cat, a chair or a cricket ball in a blend of two places. Either the rules change at some size, or something else hides the quantum behaviour. Different interpretations pick different answers (previous lesson).
The environment is always looking

A real system is never alone. A dust grain is bombarded by air molecules and light. Each tiny contact records a little information about where the grain is. That information, scattered into the environment, is the same as "watching" in the double-slit experiment: the stripes disappear. H. Dieter Zeh (1970) and Wojciech Zurek (from 1981) developed this idea. The coherence needed for interference leaks away into countless environment particles.
Spilling ink into a river

A drop of ink in a bucket swirls into patterns you could in principle reverse. Dropped into a river, the ink spreads so widely it is lost for ever in practice. Where it breaks: in decoherence the information is not destroyed, only spread out. Strictly, the whole thing plus environment is still a superposition.
Honest limits

It explains Why everyday objects look classical, why the stripes vanish, how fast the quantum look fades (extremely fast for big warm things). It does not explain Why you see one outcome. After decoherence the mix looks like "either this or that", but you still need an interpretation (many-worlds, collapse, pilot wave) to say why one happens.
Watching decoherence happen

Serge Haroche (Paris, 1996): atoms in a cavity made tiny "Schrödinger kitten" states, and watched them decohere in milliseconds. Haroche and David Wineland shared the 2012 Nobel. Arndt, Zeilinger and others: heating C60 molecules makes them radiate and the stripes fade, as predicted. 2025 Nobel (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis): quantum behaviour in a large circuit. Quantum computers: engineers fight decoherence daily; qubits last microseconds to milliseconds in superconducting devices.
Myths to drop

"The cat is both dead and alive." By decoherence, within a fraction of a second the box is not in a sharp blend; what remains is the interpretation question. "A conscious observer is needed." A cat counts as an environment, and so does a stray photon. "Decoherence solves the measurement problem." Not alone.
GKSL and Indian qubit labs

E.C.G. Sudarshan is a co-author (with Gorini and Kossakowski, 1976) of the GKSL equation (also called Lindblad), the standard mathematical description of how a quantum system loses coherence. It is used by every quantum computing group worldwide, including the labs at TIFR and IISc under the National Quantum Mission.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Schrödinger's cat (1935) was a challenge to stretching quantum rules to big objects. Decoherence (Zeh, Zurek) explains why big warm things look classical. It hides the blend but does not by itself say why one outcome occurs. Think about it Why does a cold, isolated atom stay quantum longer than a warm cat? Why is decoherence the main enemy of quantum computers?
Quantum Field Theory in Plain Words
What the particles really are

Quantum mechanics treats particles as given. But particles can be created and destroyed: a photon is born when an atom drops a level, an electron and its antiparticle appear from energy. A theory that tracks a fixed number of particles cannot handle that. Quantum field theory (QFT) fixes this by saying: fields are the real thing, and particles are ripples in them.
A field for each kind of particle

A field is a quantity with a value at every point of space, like temperature in a room. QFT says there is an electron field everywhere, a photon (electromagnetic) field everywhere, a quark field and so on. A particle is the smallest possible ripple of its field. All electrons are identical because they are ripples in the same field. That finally explains why identical particles have no individual identity.
Waves on the sea

Think of the sea: one surface, many waves. A wave can be made or vanish, but the water remains. Fields are the sea; particles are the waves. Where it breaks: the sea is made of water molecules. The fields are not made of anything, and their ripples come in whole counts: one electron, two electrons, never one and a half.
Dirac and the positron

Paul Dirac's 1928 equation joined quantum mechanics with special relativity, and demanded a partner for the electron with the same mass but opposite charge. Carl Anderson found this positron in cosmic-ray tracks in 1932. Every particle has an antiparticle (some, like the photon, are their own). Matter and antimatter can annihilate to energy, and energy can make pairs. This is how PET scans work.
The best-tested theory

Quantum electrodynamics, the QFT of light and charge, was completed in the late 1940s by Richard Feynman, Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga (Nobel 1965). Its predictions include the Lamb shift (1947) and the electron's magnetism (g-2), which agree with experiment to about ten or more decimal places, one of the most accurate matches in science.
The full catalogue

The Standard Model is QFT with 17 particle types: matter fermions (quarks, electrons and their relatives, neutrinos), force-carrying bosons (photon, gluon, W and Z) and the Higgs boson. The Higgs field gives mass to particles; the boson was found at CERN's LHC in 2012. The model leaves out gravity, dark matter and dark energy, and cannot explain why neutrinos have mass.
Empty space is not empty

Even with no particles, fields have a lowest-energy state with constant fluctuations. The Casimir effect (predicted 1948) is a tiny force between two metal plates caused by this, measured in 1997 by Steve Lamoreaux. But adding up the vacuum energy predicts a cosmological constant about 10¹²⁰ times larger than what astronomers see: one of the worst mismatches in physics, still unsolved.
Experiments

Positron, 1932; the muon, pions and many particles in accelerators. Electron g-2 matched to about 12 digits. W and Z bosons at CERN (1983). Higgs boson (ATLAS and CMS, 2012). The muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab: its final 2025 result agrees closely with the Standard Model prediction when updated calculations are used; as of 2025 the earlier tension has largely faded.
Myths to drop

"Virtual particles are tiny balls popping in and out." They are a bookkeeping device in calculations, not things you could catch. "The vacuum has endless usable energy." You cannot extract it. "Fields are made of aether." They are not a medium; they are the basic stuff.
Bhabha and CERN

Homi J. Bhabha calculated how electrons and positrons scatter from each other in 1935; it is still called Bhabha scattering , and it is used to measure collider brightness. With Walter Heitler he explained cosmic-ray showers (1937). S.N. Bose's photon counting is the root of boson statistics. India became an associate member of CERN in January 2017, and Indian groups take part in the CMS and ALICE experiments.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

QFT: fields are basic; particles are quantised ripples. Dirac (1928) predicted antimatter; QED matches experiment to many digits. Standard Model: 17 particles including Higgs (2012). It omits gravity. Think about it Why does QFT explain that all electrons are identical? Why is the vacuum energy mismatch such a puzzle?
Quantum Technologies: Lasers, MRI, Transistors
You are holding quantum technology

Quantum theory is not only for labs. Estimates often say a large fraction of the world's economy depends on technology built on it. This lesson covers the "first quantum revolution": devices that use quantum rules of matter. The "second revolution" (computers, cryptography, sensors that use superposition and entanglement) follows.
Why materials differ

In a solid, atoms' energy levels merge into wide bands . Electrons fill bands from the bottom, obeying the Pauli principle. If the highest filled band is full and there is a gap above, the material is an insulator or semiconductor. If a band is partly filled, it conducts. Doping silicon with a little phosphorus or boron tunes it. At Bell Labs in December 1947, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley built the first transistor (Nobel 1956). Today a phone chip has billions of transistors.
Light in lockstep

Einstein (1917) showed that an excited atom hit by a photon can emit a second identical photon: stimulated emission. Fill a material with excited atoms between two mirrors and you get a chain reaction of identical photons: a laser. Theodore Maiman built the first (ruby, 1960); Townes, Basov and Prokhorov won the 1964 Nobel for the principle. Photons are bosons, so they pile into the same state. Lasers drive fibre-optic internet, barcode scanners, eye surgery and cutting tools.
Seeing with spins

Body tissue is rich in hydrogen, and each hydrogen nucleus has spin. In a strong magnetic field they line up; a radio pulse tips them; as they relax they send back a signal that depends on the tissue. Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield turned this into imaging (1970s; Nobel 2003). No ionising radiation is used.
Counting atoms' vibrations

Atoms of one kind are identical, so their energy gap is a perfect ruler. Since 1967 the second has been defined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation from a caesium-133 atom. Atomic clocks make GPS and mobile networks work: GPS needs timing to billionths of a second. Optical clocks now keep time to about one second in billions of years.
Everyday quantum

LEDs and solar cells: photon energies set by band gaps. Flash memory: tunnelling. Magnetic hard disks: giant magnetoresistance (Fert and Gruenberg, Nobel 2007). Electron microscopes: matter waves. Chemistry and drugs: quantum rules of bonds.
Why it is trusted

Each device is a test. A transistor works only if band theory is right. A laser works only if stimulated emission exists. Atomic clocks agree with each other to many digits. These are daily, industrial-scale tests of the same theory.
Myths to drop

"Quantum technology means quantum computers." Most quantum technology is already in your pocket. "A laser is a special type of light bulb." A bulb gives random photons; a laser gives matched ones. "MRI uses radiation like X-rays." It uses magnetic fields and radio waves.
Patel, Raman, NavIC

C.K.N. Patel, an Indian-born engineer at Bell Labs, invented the carbon dioxide laser in 1964; it is used in industry and surgery. C.V. Raman's effect is the basis of Raman spectroscopy. India's own navigation system NavIC uses atomic clocks built into its satellites (ISRO's rubidium clocks, with some early failures in 2016-17). India's semiconductor mission, launched in 2021-22, aims to build chip fabs at home.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Band theory (Pauli plus waves) explains conductors, insulators and transistors (1947). Lasers rely on stimulated emission; MRI on nuclear spin; clocks on atomic levels. This first quantum revolution powers the modern economy. Think about it Why does a small band gap make silicon useful as a switch? Why are photons in a laser all alike?
Quantum Computing
A different kind of machine

A classical computer stores bits: 0 or 1. A quantum computer stores qubits , which can be in a superposition of 0 and 1. Linked by entanglement, they might solve some problems (not all) vastly faster. Big claims surround this field. Here is what is solid and what is hype.
What changes

Two ordinary bits hold one of four values. Two qubits hold a blend of four values at once, with amplitudes. With n qubits, there are 2ⁿ amplitudes: 300 qubits would need more numbers than there are atoms in the visible universe to describe. This is the reason a classical computer cannot easily simulate a big quantum one. Richard Feynman (1981) pointed out that to simulate quantum nature efficiently, you need a computer that is itself quantum. David Deutsch (1985) gave the first formal model.
Not "all answers at once"

A common myth says a quantum computer tries every answer at the same time. Measuring gives just one random result. The art is to design steps so that wrong answers cancel and the right one adds up , using interference.
What they offer

Shor (1994): factors large numbers in a number of steps that grows only polynomially. Classical methods grow far faster. It would break the RSA and elliptic-curve encryption used online. Grover (1996): searches an unsorted list of N items in about √N steps rather than N: a speed-up, but only a square-root one. Simulation of molecules and materials : possibly the most useful near-term target.
The race

Qubit types: superconducting circuits (Google, IBM), trapped ions (Quantinuum, IonQ), neutral atoms, photons, and spins in silicon. Google's 2019 Sycamore (53 qubits) claimed "quantum supremacy": a task in 200 seconds that they estimated would take a supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM disputed this, and later classical methods narrowed the gap. The task had no practical use. In December 2024 Google's Willow chip (105 qubits) showed that adding qubits could reduce errors, a key milestone for error correction.
The real obstacle

Qubits are fragile: decoherence and noisy gates cause errors in roughly one in a thousand steps at best. Quantum error correction combines many physical qubits into one reliable "logical qubit". A 2025 estimate by Craig Gidney (Google) suggested breaking RSA-2048 might need fewer than one million noisy qubits running for about a week, a big reduction from older estimates, but today's machines have hundreds to a few thousand qubits, not millions.
Where it stands (as of 2026)

Machines exist and are improving fast, but, to the best of public knowledge, they have not yet beaten classical computers at a commercially useful task by a clear margin. Cryptographically relevant machines are not expected for years; timelines vary widely and are uncertain.
Myths to drop

"It tries all answers at once." It uses interference to steer. "It will replace your laptop." It helps only with special problems. "It can break all encryption tomorrow." Not yet; and new post-quantum codes exist.
QpiAI and the Mission

In April 2025 the Bengaluru start-up QpiAI launched QpiAI-Indus, billed as India's first full-stack 25-qubit superconducting quantum computer. A larger machine has been announced. India's National Quantum Mission (approved April 2023) sets a goal of 50 to 1,000 physical qubits over eight years. TIFR and IISc are building superconducting qubits; the IISc-led hub focuses on computing.
Key takeaways and think-about-it

Qubits use superposition and entanglement; algorithms use interference. Shor (1994) threatens RSA; Grover (1996) gives a square-root speed-up. Error correction is the main hurdle; practical advantage is not yet broad (as of 2026). Think about it Why does measuring a quantum computer give only one answer? Why can 300 qubits not be simulated classically?
Quantum Cryptography and India's Quantum Mission
Codes that rest on physics, not on hard sums

Today's online security (RSA and elliptic curves) depends on maths problems being hard. Shor's algorithm shows a big quantum computer could crack them. Two answers: quantum key distribution (QKD), which uses physics to detect spies, and post-quantum cryptography , which uses new maths hard even for quantum machines. India's National Quantum Mission pursues both ideas.
The key rule

You cannot make a perfect copy of an unknown quantum state. This no-cloning theorem was proved in 1982 by William Wootters and Wojciech Zurek, and independently by Dennis Dieks. It means a spy cannot copy a quantum message to read later; reading it unavoidably disturbs it.
The first QKD scheme

In 1984 Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard proposed BB84. Alice sends photons, each prepared in one of two randomly chosen "bases" (like measuring spin along two different axes). Bob measures in randomly chosen bases. Afterwards, over an ordinary channel, they reveal only which bases were used and keep the bits where they matched.
